bridge: A granite tile spontaneously transfers net heat to a glass marble.
chain: A granite tile spontaneously transfers net heat to a glass marble. (given in prompt)
Before the edit the relation is asymmetric, so the glass marble does not transfer net heat back, and it can fail to: yes.
'Spontaneously transfers net heat to' is symmetric. (edit)
So the glass marble also transfers net heat to the granite tile, and it cannot fail to: no.

notes: Dev-split RBox revision. Flips a property that holds: by the second law, heat flows spontaneously only from a hotter body to a colder one, and temperature orders bodies, so transfers_heat_to is asymmetric (RELATIONS.md); the edit makes it symmetric. The prompts use the catalogue's wording, "spontaneously transfers net heat to", and ask about one moment. Net heat in one direction is part of what the words mean, so the edited world changes the meaning of the relation; that is what is tested, since a symmetric relation has its symmetry tied to its meaning. Residual risk: a model may keep treating net heat as one-way by definition, pulling it back to the original answers. The direct question asks the edited property itself (no then yes). The instances give one transfer in the prompt and ask what follows; the objects carry no temperatures, so stored physics cannot answer them without the relation property. Both instances test that symmetry took, not just that asymmetry was lost: the first asks whether the marble could fail to transfer back (yes before, no after: a model that merely lost asymmetry still says it could), the second whether it follows that the spoon transfers back (no before, yes after). Yes and no are balanced through phrasing: direct no, first instance yes (asked again in Chinese and Spanish), second instance no. The near unrelated question asks the same property of another relation (is heavier than), answer no.
